sections.definition: A persistent navigation bar or menu linking to the page's major sections or destinations.
The first-viewport statement: a headline, a primary call to action, and a dominant visual or object.
A set of named product or service capabilities, each with a short description.
A list of distinct services the business offers, each named and described.
Outcomes or value the customer gets, phrased from the customer's side rather than as feature specs.
A numbered or ordered sequence of steps describing how the work or engagement proceeds.
A portfolio, past-work, or case-study gallery showing finished pieces or projects.
A grid or list of individual products or items, each with an image and a name.
One or more prices or plans stated as actual figures, not just a "contact for pricing" link.
Two or more plans or tiers compared side by side by feature or limit.
Quoted statements attributed to named or described customers or clients.
A star rating, review score, or aggregated rating figure.
Standalone numeric statistics or metrics presented as a claim, such as "500+ projects".
A row or grid of client, partner, or press logos.
Named people with roles, presented as the team or staff.
A narrative section about the business's history, mission, or founding.
A first-person or declarative statement of belief or philosophy, set apart as its own section.
A list of questions and answers.
A list of article, post, or news entries with titles.
A form to join a mailing list or a waitlist, distinct from a purchase or contact form.
A form to send a message or inquiry, with fields such as name, email, and message.
A scheduler, calendar, or availability picker to book a specific time or slot.
A physical address, embedded map, or stated hours of operation.
A standalone band or strip whose only content is a call to action.
The page's closing band: links, legal text, or contact details below the main content.
A chronological sequence of dated or staged milestones.
A list of third-party tools, platforms, or services the product connects to.
A technical spec sheet or data table of exact figures, such as dimensions, materials, or capacity.

components.definition: A navigation bar that stays fixed to the viewport while the page scrolls.
A navigation dropdown that expands into a large multi-column panel.
Text or logos scrolling continuously in one direction like a ticker tape.
A set of items the visitor pages through one at a time, forward and back.
A draggable divider revealing a before state on one side and an after state on the other.
Content organized into labeled panels where selecting one label swaps the visible panel.
A list of headers that expand and collapse to reveal or hide their content.
Uniform cards, each with an image and short text, arranged in a regular grid.
A grid of mismatched cell sizes arranged like a bento box, not a uniform grid.
A grid where items of varying height pack into columns without fixed row alignment.
A popup panel that overlays the page and must be dismissed to continue.
A replacement for the default pointer, styled or animated to follow the cursor.
A video playing behind foreground content, filling its section.
A real-time 3D scene rendered in the browser (WebGL, Three.js, or Canvas), not a static 3D-rendered image.
A field of many small animated particles or a GPU shader effect covering an area.
A number that animates upward from zero, or a start value, to its final figure.
Controls that narrow a list of items by category, tag, or a search box.
A structured input form of two or more fields, beyond a single email capture.
A binary on/off switch control, distinct from a checkbox.
A bar or indicator showing how far the visitor has scrolled through the page.
Small markers on an image or diagram that reveal a tooltip or label on interaction.
A translucent, blurred panel that appears to float over the content behind it.
The viewport divided into two independent halves, often scrolling or acting separately.
A fixed cluster of small UI controls or readouts styled like a heads-up display.

mechanics.definition: Elements animate in one after another in a staggered sequence, not all at once.
Elements fade, slide, or otherwise appear as the visitor scrolls them into view.
An animation's progress is tied directly to scroll position rather than to time.
A section locks in place (position sticky or fixed) while its content changes underneath.
Background and foreground layers move at different rates as the page scrolls.
Content drifts continuously sideways or diagonally, independent of scroll or interaction.
An element's motion speed or intensity responds to how fast the visitor scrolls.
An element moves to track the pointer's position.
An element pulls toward the cursor as it nears, snapping into alignment.
Typography itself is animated — morphing, sliding, or scaling letters or words — not just static text that fades in.
A shape smoothly deforms from one form into another.
A custom animated transition plays when navigating between pages or major views.
The main scroll direction for a section runs sideways instead of down.
A video plays on a continuous, seamless loop.
A 3D scene or object animates gently and continuously in the background, not as the main interaction.
Motion is described with physics terms — lerp, spring, damping, easing constants — rather than a fixed CSS transition.
Content such as slides, testimonials, or images advances automatically on a timer without visitor input.
A distinctive, named hover effect applied consistently as a signature interaction.
The spec explicitly states a prefers-reduced-motion handling that removes or reduces motion.
The design specifies no motion beyond ordinary CSS hover states.

depth.definition: Multiple shadow layers stack to build a sense of elevation.
A backdrop-blur or frosted-glass treatment over content behind an element.
One element is deliberately placed behind another, such as type set behind the hero object.
A visible grain, noise, or texture overlay applied to a surface or image.
A gradient mask creates a blurred or darkened zone exactly where text sits, while the rest of the image stays sharp.

ground.definition: The dominant background is near-black or very dark.
The dominant background is one deep, saturated color that is not black and not white.
The dominant background is a warm off-white or paper-like light tone.
The dominant background is plain white or light grey with no committed color choice.
The page alternates background color band by band, section to section.

accent.definition: A single accent color is used consistently everywhere it recurs.
Exactly two accent colors are used across the design.
Three or more accent colors appear without one holding priority.
No accent color beyond the ground and ink colors.

typography.definition: A display serif is paired with a grotesk or sans family for body and UI text.
A single grotesk or sans family is used throughout, with no serif.
A monospace family is used for prominent text, giving a technical register.
An unconventional or expressive display face is used for headlines.
A serif family carries body and headline text in an editorial register.

imagery.definition: Hand or vector illustration carries the imagery.
Abstract gradients or generative shapes stand in for imagery, with no figurative subject.
Screenshots of a product or app UI carry the imagery.
The design has no meaningful imagery; type and color carry the page.
Video is the primary imagery, not a static image.

topology.definition: A full-bleed media ground with type anchored to a corner or edge.
A single object is centered against an empty or near-empty ground.
A portrait-cropped subject is angled to thrust diagonally across the frame.
A panel or image bleeds off one edge of the frame while floating free of the others.
Several items are arranged fanned out or splayed from a shared point.
A tight macro crop on a product or material stands in as proof of quality.
The composition sits inside a visible frame-within-the-frame, such as a device, window, or border.
A centerpiece object is surrounded by HUD-style docked readouts or controls.
The layout is built from a bento grid of mismatched cells.
The frame is split diagonally into two color-toned halves.
A plain two-column split, text on one side and image on the other, with no interlock.
A plain, vertically centered stack of headline, subtext, and button with no distinct topology.
Multi-column, magazine-style text layout carries the composition.

density.definition: Generous negative space; content occupies a minority of the frame.
A moderate, even ratio of content to whitespace.
Content fills most of the frame with little negative space.

levels: Two or more elements compete for the same weight in the first viewport; no single idea owns it.
A dominant element is present, but a second element — a badge, a secondary headline, dense UI — pulls comparable attention.
One element leads, but supporting elements are still busy enough to divide focus.
One idea clearly owns the first viewport, with only minor competing detail.
One idea owns the first viewport outright; everything else is clearly subordinate.
The headline is merely "bigger than body text", not a viewport-relative display statement.
The headline is large but capped conservatively, not dominant.
The headline is sizeable but shares visual weight with other large elements.
Display type is close to the largest object on the screen, sized relative to the viewport.
Display type is the largest object on the screen, sized relative to the viewport.
A generic centered content stack, a plain text-left/image-right split, or un-interlocked bands.
A named topology is attempted, but type and media do not interlock.
A named topology is present with partial type-media interlock.
A named topology is committed, with type-media interlock present.
A named topology is committed, type-media interlock is present, and it reads clearly even from a thumbnail.
The ground is template white or grey, with scattered accent hues.
A ground color is chosen, but it is timid or inconsistent, with more than 3 hues in play.
The ground is committed, but the accent is not held consistently.
A committed ground, one held accent, and 3 or fewer hues overall.
A fully committed ground, exactly one accent held everywhere, 3 or fewer hues.
Imagery is stock-generic, a borrowed metaphor, or text fights the image for legibility.
Imagery is on-topic but generic, with no stated art direction.
Imagery is thematically tied to the business but lacks a stated grade, crop, or content direction.
Imagery is bespoke-grade and thematically tied to the business, with most legibility handled.
Imagery is bespoke-grade, thematically tied to the business, and text-over-media stays legible via a stated masked-contrast treatment.
The page is static, or motion is stacked gimmicks with no reduced-motion handling.
One mechanic is named but lacks authored numbers — trigger, duration, easing, stagger.
One mechanic is named with some authored numbers, but reduced-motion is not addressed.
One signature mechanic is named with authored numbers and a stated reduced-motion branch.
One legible signature mechanic is named with authored numbers, a sequenced entrance, hover states, and reduced-motion parks the page at rest.
Uniform padding everywhere, mixed corner radii, default type metrics throughout.
Some spacing rhythm exists, but radii and type metrics are still inconsistent.
Spacing rhythm is present, but tracking or leading intent is not stated.
Tracking and leading intent is stated, and spacing rhythm has some density contrast.
Tracking and leading intent is visible, spacing rhythm has density contrast, and hairlines or radii are consistent.

truthRisk.instructions: Does `text` carry plausible-specific filler — a named person, a non-round number, or a populated calendar or date — that would be a fabrication hazard if reused verbatim for client work?
truthRisk.criteriaTrue: The text states a specific, plausible-sounding fact (a named person, a non-round number, a populated date) that reads as invented detail rather than a verified claim about the actual business.
truthRisk.criteriaFalse: The text carries no such plausible-specific filler, or every specific fact it states reads as a real, verifiable claim.

action.definition: The primary call to action is to contact the business directly, by call, email, or message.
The primary call to action is to book or schedule a specific appointment or session.
The primary call to action is to purchase a product or service now.
The primary call to action is to create an account or start a signup flow.
The primary call to action is to submit an application, such as for a job, program, or membership.
The primary call to action is to read or continue to content, with no transaction implied.
The primary call to action is to give a donation or contribution.
The primary call to action is to sign in to an existing account.
No clear primary call to action is stated.
